lessons.title: English is stress-timed
lessons.explain: Stressed syllables land on a steady beat. The weak syllables between them get squeezed to keep the timing.
points: Tap the table on each capital letter.
Keep the beats even, however many small words sit between them.

items.text: DOGS EAT BONES.
The DOGS will EAT the BONES.
The DOGS will have EAten the BONES.
I'll SEE you at the STAtion at SEven.

lessons.title: Rhythm in real conversation
lessons.explain: Shadow these lines and copy the timing before you worry about the individual sounds.
points: Keep the weak words fast and quiet.
Do not add a pause after every word.

items.text: I was gonna call you, but I got stuck at work.
To be honest, I'd rather stay home tonight.
It depends on how much time we've got.

lessons.title: Counting beats, not syllables
lessons.explain: A sentence with more words can still have the same number of beats — that's the key idea of stress-timing.

items.text: JOHN likes TEA.
JOHN would like some TEA.
JOHN would have liked some TEA.

lessons.title: Tongue twisters for rhythm control
lessons.explain: Tongue twisters force you to keep a steady rhythm even when the sounds are tricky — slow down before speeding up.

items.text: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.
She sells seashells by the seashore.
items.pattern: SHE SELLS SEAshells by the SEAshore

items.text: Red lorry, yellow lorry.

lessons.title: Rhythm in short answers
lessons.explain: Even a short answer has a natural beat — don't say every word with equal force.

items.text: Yes, I THINK so.
No, not REALly.
Sure, why NOT?

lessons.title: Rhythm in numbers and lists
lessons.explain: Reciting numbers or a list still keeps a steady beat on each stressed item.

items.text: ONE, TWO, THREE, FOUR, FIVE.
MONday, TUESday, WEDnesday.

lessons.title: Rhythm practice with nursery-rhyme patterns
lessons.explain: Simple rhymes have an obvious, exaggerated beat — great for building a feel for stress-timing.

items.text: TWINkle TWINkle LITtle STAR.
JACK and JILL went UP the HILL.

lessons.title: Rhythm in a longer natural sentence
lessons.explain: Longer sentences keep the same stress-timed feel — the weak words between beats just move faster.

items.text: I would have called you earlier, but my phone was dead all afternoon.

lessons.title: Rhythm in questions
lessons.explain: Questions keep the same stress-timed beat as statements — the question words and key content words carry the rhythm.

items.text: WHERE did you PUT the KEYS?
WHY would he DO that?

lessons.title: Rhythm buildup drill
lessons.explain: The classic buildup drill: the same core beats stay steady as you add more small words around them.

items.text: CATS CHASE MICE.
The CATS will CHASE the MICE.
The CATS would have CHASED the MICE.
The CATS would have been CHASing the MICE all NIGHT.
items.pattern: 4 beats now — one new idea added

lessons.title: Rhythm in idioms
lessons.explain: Idioms have a fixed, sing-song rhythm as a whole chunk — say them as one rhythmic unit.

items.text: BETTER late than NEVer.
ACtions speak LOUDer than WORDS.

lessons.title: Rhythm in advertising slogans
lessons.explain: Slogans are written to have a catchy, very regular beat — great, memorable rhythm practice.

items.text: JUST DO it.
Have it YOUR way.

lessons.title: How English rhythm differs from syllable-timed languages
lessons.explain: In syllable-timed languages every syllable takes roughly equal time; English is stress-timed, so only the stressed syllables are evenly spaced and everything else speeds up or slows down to fit.
points: This is why English can sound 'fast' in the unstressed parts and 'slow' on stressed words.

items.text: I want to go.
items.pattern: 3 words, 1 beat: I want to GO.

items.text: I would like to be able to go.
items.pattern: 8 words, still close to 1-2 beats: I'd LIKE to be Able to GO.

lessons.title: Rhythm giving a short toast or speech
lessons.explain: Toasts and short speeches use a slow, deliberate, evenly-spaced rhythm for effect.

items.text: To FRIENDship, to LAUGHter, and to many more YEARS together.

lessons.title: Clapping out the beat
lessons.explain: A simple physical drill: clap only on the stressed syllables while saying the sentence, keeping the claps perfectly even.

items.text: (clap) SHE (clap) LIKES (clap) TEA.
(clap) SHE would (clap) LIKE some (clap) TEA.

lessons.title: Rhythm in a fast native dialogue snippet
lessons.explain: Real fast dialogue keeps a steady stress beat even though a lot of small words are squeezed in between.

items.text: A: You comin' or what? B: Yeah, gimme a sec, I'm almost ready.
items.pattern: COMin' … WHAT / YEAH … SEC … ALmost … REAdy

lessons.title: Rhythm in a short poem
lessons.explain: Poetry often has a very deliberate, regular beat — a great way to feel stress-timing clearly.

items.text: The ROAD not TAKen MADE all the DIFference.

lessons.title: Rhythm: excited fast beats vs calm slow beats
lessons.explain: The same sentence structure can sound excited or calm just by changing the speed between beats, not the beats themselves.

items.text: WE WON the GAME!
We WON the game.

lessons.title: Rhythm with names and greetings
lessons.explain: Greeting someone by name keeps a natural two-beat rhythm.

items.text: HI, SARah!
MORNing, JOHN!

lessons.title: Rhythm in an emphatic argument
lessons.explain: Making a firm point uses stronger, more forceful beats on the key words than normal conversation.

items.text: That is NOT what I SAID.
I have TOLD you THREE times.

lessons.title: Rhythm reading numbers aloud
lessons.explain: Reading a string of numbers keeps a light, even beat on each digit or group.

items.text: oh SEven, TWO, THREE, FIVE
TWENty, FORty, SIXty

lessons.title: Rhythm in customer service scripts
lessons.explain: Service phrases have a friendly, even, welcoming rhythm.

items.text: WELcome IN, how can I HELP you toDAY?

lessons.title: Repetition drill for rhythm confidence
lessons.explain: Repeat the same short sentence five times, keeping the beat perfectly identical each time — builds automatic rhythm control.

items.text: I LIKE it. I LIKE it. I LIKE it.

lessons.title: Rhythm in a weather report
lessons.explain: Weather reports have a brisk, professional, evenly-paced rhythm.

items.text: TOday we're LOOKing at CLEAR SKIES and MILD TEMPeratures.

lessons.title: Rhythm contrast: formal vs casual delivery
lessons.explain: The same message keeps stress-timed rhythm in both registers, but casual speech squeezes the weak words much more.

items.text: I would like to request some additional information.
items.pattern: formal — weak words still fairly clear

items.text: Can you send me more info?

lessons.title: Rhythm with consonant-cluster tongue twisters
lessons.explain: Harder tongue twisters test whether you can keep the beat steady even when individual sounds are tricky.

items.text: Six thick thistle sticks.
Trucks try to track the tracks.
items.pattern: TRUCKS TRY to TRACK the TRACKS

lessons.title: Rhythm across a two-sentence mini exchange
lessons.explain: Practise keeping a natural beat across a full back-and-forth exchange, not just one sentence.

items.text: A: WHAT time is the MEETing? B: It's at THREE, I THINK.

lessons.title: Rhythm in giving commands
lessons.explain: Short commands keep a punchy, even beat on each key word.

items.text: STOP right THERE.
SIT down and LISten.

lessons.title: Rhythm reading a menu aloud
lessons.explain: Reading menu items keeps a light, even rhythm on each dish name.

items.text: GRILLED SALmon, ROAST CHICKen, VEGgie PASta.

lessons.title: Rhythm in a simple children's song
lessons.explain: Children's songs have an exaggerated, super-regular beat — perfect for feeling stress-timing.

items.text: ROW, ROW, ROW your BOAT.

lessons.title: Rhythm mini-dialogue with contrastive stress
lessons.explain: Practise keeping even beats even when a word is extra-stressed for contrast.

items.text: A: Did SHE call you? B: No, HE called me.

lessons.title: Rhythm plus linking combined
lessons.explain: Real fluent speech combines a steady beat with linked, reduced words between the beats.

items.text: I WANna GO to the STORE.

lessons.title: Rhythm in famous movie quotes
lessons.explain: Iconic movie lines have a very deliberate, memorable rhythm — great, fun practice material.

items.text: MAY the FORCE be with YOU.
I'll be BACK.

lessons.title: Rhythm building intensity across a short speech
lessons.explain: A motivational speech often speeds up and strengthens the beats as it builds toward the end.

items.text: We CAN do this. We WILL do this. We're GOing to WIN.
items.pattern: beats get stronger and closer together

lessons.title: Rhythm in group chants and cheers
lessons.explain: Chants use a very simple, repeated, rock-solid beat.

items.text: LET'S GO TEAM! LET'S GO TEAM!

lessons.title: Rhythm with alliteration
lessons.explain: Alliterative phrases (repeated starting sounds) still follow the same stress-timed beat rules.

items.text: BIG BLUE BALLoons BOUNCED by.

lessons.title: Rhythm describing a weather map
lessons.explain: Weather-map narration has a brisk, list-like rhythm moving from region to region.

items.text: RAIN in the NORTH, SUN in the SOUTH, CLOUDS in beTWEEN.

lessons.title: Rhythm reading a recipe step by step
lessons.explain: Recipe steps have a calm, even beat guiding the listener through each action.

items.text: MIX the FLOUR, ADD the EGGS, STIR it WELL.

lessons.title: Rhythm and pausing combined drill
lessons.explain: Even with a pause between chunks, the beat inside each chunk should still feel steady and even.

items.text: When I WAS a KID / I LOVED to CLIMB TREES.
items.pattern: even beats within each chunk, pause between

lessons.title: Rhythm giving genuine compliments
lessons.explain: Compliments keep a warm, even beat on the praised quality.

items.text: That's a GREAT idea!
You did REALly WELL.

lessons.title: Rhythm counting objects
lessons.explain: Counting things aloud naturally falls into a light, even beat.

items.text: ONE apple, TWO oranges, THREE bananas.

lessons.title: Rhythm describing a daily schedule
lessons.explain: Schedule descriptions keep an even beat on each time and activity.

items.text: MEETing at NINE, LUNCH at NOON, GYM at SIX.

lessons.title: Rhythm in short exclaimed reactions
lessons.explain: Quick reactions have a snappy, single strong beat.

items.text: NO way!
So COOL!

lessons.title: Rhythm in minimal-word answers
lessons.explain: Even a one- or two-word answer carries a clear beat, not a flat mumble.

items.text: PRObably.
NOT REALly.

lessons.title: Rhythm in a radio advertisement
lessons.explain: Radio ads use an energetic, punchy, very regular beat to stay memorable.

items.text: COME on DOWN to SUPer SAVE, where PRICes NEVer STOP FALLing!

lessons.title: Rhythm building from one word to a full sentence
lessons.explain: Start with just the stressed word, then rebuild the full sentence around it, keeping that word's beat unchanged.

items.text: GO.
Let's GO.
I think we should GO now.

lessons.title: Rhythm in a short apology speech
lessons.explain: A sincere apology keeps a slow, steady, even beat — rushing it can sound insincere.

items.text: I'm SORry. I was WRONG. It won't HAPpen aGAIN.

lessons.title: Rhythm reading a short news headline
lessons.explain: News headlines are read with clear, confident, evenly-spaced beats on the key facts.

items.text: CITY COUNcil APproves NEW PARK PLAN.

lessons.title: Rhythm: yes/no answer plus a quick follow-up
lessons.explain: A short answer plus a quick extra detail still keeps one connected, even rhythm.

items.text: YEAH, I'm PRETty SURE.

lessons.title: Rhythm in a short farewell speech
lessons.explain: A warm goodbye speech uses a slow, even, heartfelt beat, similar to a toast.

items.text: It's been an HONor WORKing with all of YOU.
